name: Hmong Dô
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Only Niederer 1998 (comparative Hmong-Mien) cited; no description of Hmong Do (Vietnam) stress located

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 page for Hmong Dô (hmon1332) and hh.bib entries with language code hmv
sources.note: No dialects, no descriptive references; alt names Hmong Do, Hmo, Hmung, Hsiung, Hunan Miao. hh.bib note on Caelen-Haumont 2012: Mo Piu 'very good candidate for to be equated with = Hmong Dô [hmv]'; Niederer language code glosses hmv as 'Hmong Du = Black Hmong mainly in northwestern Lao Cai and northeastern Lai Chau'.

Nothing on stress. States Mo Piu has no ISO code, ~240 speakers (2011), and that Ly Van Tu & Vittrant (2014, SEALS 24) tentatively classify it as a Guiyang Miao dialect; lists the four Caelen-Haumont papers.

sources.citation: Caelen-Haumont, G. & K. Bartkova. 2013. Manual and automatic tone annotation: the case of an endangered language from North Vietnam 'Mo Piu'. Proc. Interspeech 2013 (Lyon), 1448-1452. doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2013-377
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Tone patterns from a prototone word list: mainly falling /41, 43, 54/ and plateau /33/; 206 (often compound) words; nothing on prominence within compounds.

sources.citation: Caelen-Haumont, G. & S. Sam. 2012. Comparison between two models of language for the automatic phonetic labeling of an undocumented language of the South-Asia: the case of Mo Piu. Proc. LREC 2012 (Istanbul), 956-962.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; speech-technology paper on automatic phonetic labeling; only repeats that Mo Piu belongs to Hmong-Mien as an unknown branch.

sources.citation: Caelen-Haumont, G. 2012. Towards the Mo Piu tonal system: first results on an undocumented South-Asian language. Proc. Speech Prosody 2012 (Shanghai), 119-122. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2012-33
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent (a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/intensity empty). Syllable structure C(C)V(C,V) with prenasalised onsets; isolated-word tones /22, 33, 21, 32, 42, 43, 54, 43-32/, no rising tone; compared with White Hmong tones (Niederer).

sources.citation: Caelen-Haumont, G. 2012. Towards the tonal system of an unknown language from South-East Asia: a deeper insight. Proc. TAL 2012 (Nanjing), paper P1-15, 6 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. p. 1: 'It seems until now that most of the lexical units are monosyllabic'; previous study showed 'the language was mainly monosyllabic, 2° it was tonal, 3° there were existing many tones in the shape of a plateau'. Only 'accented' appears in a generic remark about MISTRAL+ handling accented vs tonal languages.

sources.citation: Caelen-Haumont, G., B. Cortial, C. Culas, Tran Tri Doi, Thom Dinh Hong, Xuyen Le Thi, Hung Phan Luong, Thanh Nguyen Ngoc, E. Pannier, V. Roux, J.-P. Salmon, A. Vittrant, Hoang Thi Vuong & Ly A Song. 2010. Mo Piu minority language: data base, first steps and first experiments. Proc. SLTU 2010 (Penang), 42-50.
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. First description of the language: from syllable durations (mean 378 ms) and the abundance of F0 plateaux concludes (p. 48-49) that Mo Piu is 'tonal and monosyllabic'; word = syllable; 3-4 level plateau tones plus falling and rising contours; duration possibly lexically relevant.

sources.citation: Ly Van Tu & Alice Vittrant. 2014. Place of Mơ Piu in the Hmong group: a proposal. Paper presented at SEALS 24, Yangon, Myanmar.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The one linguist-authored (LACITO) sketch of Mo Piu; would settle whether Mo Piu is a Guiyang Miao dialect (per Wikipedia's report of it) rather than hmv, and likely gives a phoneme/tone inventory with any remarks on prosody.
